There is no fault. The <s>ācārya</s>, by saying 'northward and southward,' indicates the already-established equatorial circle. For otherwise, 'northward and southward' would be meaningless. And the words 'north' and 'south' express direction, and direction is determined by reference [to a baseline]. Therefore, having first established the equatorial circle, the ecliptic circle is then established. All circles should be made marked with three-hundred-sixty [divisions], since the zodiacal circle consists of three-hundred-sixty degrees. // 1 //

body.text: apakramamaṇḍalacāriṇaḥ
body.translated_text: Those that travel on the ecliptic circle

body.text: tasmin ca apakramamaṇḍale ke bhramanti iti āha ã
body.translated_text: And on that ecliptic circle, who revolves? He says:

children.text: tārāgrahendupātāḥ bhramanti ajasram apamaṇḍale arkaḥ ca |
children.translated_text: The star-planets (<s>tārāgrahas</s>), the Moon's nodes (<s>indupātas</s>), revolve constantly on the ecliptic (<s>apamaṇḍala</s>), and the Sun too;

children.text: arkāt ca maṇḍalārdhe bhramati hi tasmin kṣiticchāyā || 2 ||
children.translated_text: and from the Sun, at a half-circle [distance], the Earth's shadow revolves on that [ecliptic]. // 2 //

body.text:
tārāgrahāḥ bhaumabudhabṛhaspatiśukraśanaiścarāḥ, tārāgrahendupātāḥ bhramanti ajasram avyavacchedena, apamaṇḍale apakramamaṇḍale, arkaḥ ca na kevalam ete tārāgrahendupātāḥ apamaṇḍale bhramanti, arkaḥ ca | tatra apamaṇḍale ajasram arkaḥ ca bhramati | arkāt ca maṇḍalārdhe arkāt punar maṇḍalārdhe ṣaḍrāśyantare, bhramati hi tasmin tatra maṇḍalārdhe, bhūcchāyā | yathā stambhādīnām pradīpavaśāt chāyā bhramati, evam bhuvaḥ api arkavaśāt,
na kevalam tārāgrahendupātāḥ iti |
body.translated_text: The star-planets are Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn. The star-planets and Moon's nodes revolve constantly — without interruption — on the ecliptic, the <s>apamaṇḍala</s> (ecliptic circle), and the Sun too. Not only do these star-planets and Moon's nodes revolve on the ecliptic, but the Sun as well. There, on the ecliptic, the Sun revolves constantly. And from the Sun, at a half-circle [distance] — at an interval of six signs — the Earth's shadow (<s>bhūcchāyā</s>) revolves on that [ecliptic], on that half-circle. Just as the shadows of pillars and such revolve due to a lamp, so too the Earth's [shadow revolves] due to the Sun — not only the star-planets and Moon's nodes [revolve on the ecliptic].

body.text:
pātānām apakramamaṇḍale gatiḥ uktā | tat kim idānīm arkāt maṇḍalārdhe bhūcchāyā bhramati iti ucyate | na ca bhūcchāyāvyatiriktaḥ pātaḥ asti candramasaḥ | na eṣaḥ doṣaḥ | sarveṣām eva tārāgrahāṇām ye pātāḥ te apakramamaṇḍale bhramanti | candramasaḥ punar pātaḥ arkāt maṇḍalārdhe apakramamaṇḍale bhramati iti etat eva artham | "arkāt ca maṇḍalārdhe bhramati hi tasmin kṣiticchāyā" iti kathayati | nanu ca budhādīnām ye pātāḥ te niścalāḥ teṣām
niścalānām katham apakramamaṇḍalagatiḥ ucyate ? na te niścalāḥ, "navarāṣaha gatvā aṃśakān prathamapātāḥ" [gītikāí, 9] iti atra "gatvā"-śabdena teṣām gatyupadeśāt |
body.translated_text: The motion of the nodes on the ecliptic (<s>apakramamaṇḍala</s>) has been stated. Now, is it being said that the Earth's shadow revolves at half-a-circle from the Sun? But there is no node of the Moon other than the Earth's shadow. There is no fault here — the nodes of all the star-planets revolve on the ecliptic. Moreover, the node of the Moon revolves on the ecliptic at half-a-circle from the Sun — this is the very meaning. He says 'the Earth's shadow revolves on it at half-a-circle from the Sun.' But [objection:] the nodes of Mercury and the like are stationary — how can their motion on the ecliptic be stated? They are not stationary, because in [the statement] 'having traversed <s>na-va-rā-ṣa-ha</s> degrees, the first nodes' [<s>Gītikā</s> 9], their motion is taught by the word 'having traversed.'

body.text:
"tārāgrahendupātāḥ" iti iyam āryā kim artham ārabhyate? tārāgrahādīnām gatiḥ apakramamaṇḍale vijñāyate | uktam ca "bhāpakramaḥ grahāṃśāḥ" [gītikāí, 8] iti sarve[ṣām gatimatā]m ete apakramabhāgāḥ iti | yadi ca gītikoktam api atra punar ucyate, tadā tarhi bahu atra abhidheyam iti | athavā raveḥ cakrārdhe bhūcchāyā bhramati iti etat pradarśayitavyam syāt, tat ca na pradeśāntarapradarśitatvāt | "bhūravivivaram vibhajet" [golaí, 39] iti atra pradīpacchāyopapatyā
bhūcchāyānayanam upadiśet | raveḥ cakrārdhe bhūcchāyā bhramati iti etat pradarśayati, yataḥ hi śaṅkaḥ ṛjusthitasya pradīpasya tat ṛjupravṛttacchāyā | tasmāt iyam āryā ārabdhavyā iti || 2 ||
body.translated_text: For what purpose is this <s>āryā</s> 'the star-planets and Moon-nodes' commenced? The motion of the star-planets and the like is known to be on the ecliptic. And it has been said: 'the declination of the stars, the degrees of the planets' [<s>Gītikā</s> 8] — these are the ecliptic degrees of all moving [bodies]. If what was stated in the <s>Gītikā</s> is being repeated here, then there would be much to state here. Or else, it would be needed to demonstrate that the Earth's shadow revolves at half-a-circle from the Sun, and that is not [established elsewhere] since it has not been shown in another passage. In [the verse] 'divide the Earth-Sun distance' [<s>Gola</s> 39], the computation of the Earth's shadow should be taught through the lamp-shadow analogy. He demonstrates that the Earth's shadow revolves at half-a-circle from the Sun — for the shadow of a gnomon placed in a straight line from a lamp extends straight. Therefore, this <s>āryā</s> must be commenced. // 2 //

body.text: vikṣepamaṇḍalacāriṇaḥ
body.translated_text: Those moving on the deflection-circle

body.text: grahāṇām vikṣepamaṇḍalapradarśanāya āha ã
body.translated_text: In order to demonstrate the deflection-circles (<s>vikṣepamaṇḍala</s>) of the planets, he says:

children.text: apamaṇḍalasya candraḥ pātāt yāti uttareṇa dakṣiṇataḥ |
children.translated_text: The Moon moves from the node northward and southward of the ecliptic (<s>apamaṇḍala</s>);

children.text: kujagurukoṇāḥ ca evam śīghroccena api budhaśukrau || 3 ||
children.translated_text: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn likewise; and Mercury and Venus also by their fast apogee (<s>śīghrocca</s>). // 3 //

body.text:
apamaṇḍalasya | apamaṇḍalam apakramamaṇḍalam | apakramamaṇḍalasya candraḥ | apamaṇḍalasaṃbandhī candraḥ "apamaṇḍalasya candraḥ" iti ucyate | apamaṇḍalasaṃsthitaḥ vā candraḥ apamaṇḍalasya candraḥ, yathā ã kusūlasya vrīhayaḥ | athavā adhikaraṇārthā iyam ṣaṣṭhī, yataḥ hi ekaśatam ṣaṣṭhyarthāḥ, apamaṇḍale candraḥ iti etasmin arthe | sa apamaṇḍalavyavasthitaḥ candraḥ pātāt yāti gacchati | pātaśabdena candramasaḥ vikṣepāpakramamaṇḍalayoḥ saṃyogaḥ
abhidhīyate | tasya ca saṃyogasya pratikṣaṇam gatimattvāt, sā gatiḥ pātaśabdena abhidhīyate, upacārāt | ataḥ sa gatisaṃjñitaḥ pātaḥ yasmin rāśau yāvatithe bhāge vartate tasmin rāśau tāvatithe bhāge apakramamaṇḍalapramāṇam eva anyat maṇḍalam tasmin badhvā dvitīyam ardham cakrārdhāntare tathā eva badhnīyāt yathā tat apakramamaṇḍalāt uttareṇa avatiṣṭhate tasya [prathamam ardham], yathā dvitīyam ardham vā dakṣiṇena upalakṣyate | evam ca prathamapātāt
apakramamaṇḍalasya uttareṇa vikṣepamaṇḍalam, dvitīyapātāt ca dakṣiṇena, ubhayatra cakracaturbhāgāntare yathā ardhapañcamāḥ bhāgāḥ tasya ca apakramamaṇḍalasya antare bhavanti tathā badhnīyāt vikṣepamaṇḍalam | tasmin candramāḥ bhramati | viṣuvataḥ uttareṇa dakṣiṇena vā tat apakramamaṇḍalam | tasmāt apakramamaṇḍalāt uttareṇa dakṣiṇena vā vikṣepamaṇḍalam pradarśayet |
body.translated_text: 'Of the ecliptic' (<s>apamaṇḍalasya</s>): the <s>apamaṇḍala</s> is the ecliptic (<s>apakramamaṇḍala</s>). 'The Moon of the ecliptic' — the Moon connected with the ecliptic is called 'the Moon of the ecliptic.' Or, the Moon situated on the ecliptic [is so called], like 'the grains of the granary.' Alternatively, this is a sixth-case [genitive] in the locative sense, since there are a hundred [possible senses of the genitive] — meaning 'the Moon on the ecliptic.' That Moon, situated on the ecliptic, 'moves from the node' — goes from the node. By the word 'node' (<s>pāta</s>), the conjunction of the Moon's deflection-circle and the ecliptic is denoted. And since that conjunction moves at every instant, that motion is denoted by the word 'node,' by convention. Therefore, at whatever sign and at whatever degree that node designated as 'motion' is situated — at that sign and that degree, one should bind another circle of the same measure as the ecliptic, and bind the second half at the [point] half-a-circle away such that the first half stands to the north of the ecliptic, while the second half is observed to the south. Thus, from the first node, the deflection-circle is to the north of the ecliptic, and from the second node, to the south; at a quarter-circle from both [nodes], it should be bound at the deflection-circle such that four and a half degrees lie within the interval of the ecliptic. On that [deflection-circle], the Moon revolves. The ecliptic is to the north or south of the equator (<s>viṣuvat</s>). From that ecliptic, the deflection-circle should be shown to the north or south.

body.text:
candrasya ca vikṣepamaṇḍalavyavasthitasya viṣuvataḥ ca antarānayane iyam yuktiḥ ã sphuṭacandramasaḥ bhujajyayā trairāśikam ã yadi vyāsārdhatulyayā bhujajyayā caturviṃśatyapakramabhāgajyā labhyate tataḥ candrabhujajyayā kā iti, apakramabhāgajyā labhyate | tataḥ pātāt apakramamaṇḍalavyavasthitaḥ candraḥ dakṣiṇena uttareṇa vā yāti iti uktavān | pātāvadhi parijñānāya sphuṭacandramasaḥ pātaḥ viśodhyate, tatra viśeṣasya yā jyā tayā trairāśikam ã yadi
vyāsārdhajyayā candravikṣepabhāgajyā labhyate anayā iṣṭajyayā kā iti, iṣṭavikṣepajyā labhyate | tayoḥ vikṣepāpakramajyayoḥ kāṣṭhīkṛtayoḥ tulyadikkayoḥ yogaḥ, yasmāt apakramamaṇḍalāt parataḥ candraḥ vartate | bhinnadikkayoḥ viśeṣaḥ, yasmāt ārāt apakramamaṇḍalā[t vikṣepamaṇḍalam] candraḥ ca | gole yathārtham pradarśayet | yogaviśleṣabhāgānām yā jyā tāvat antaram viṣuvataḥ candramasaḥ ca | jyāpramāṇena kāṣṭhapramāṇam uktam |
body.translated_text: And for determining the interval between the Moon situated on the deflection-circle and the equator, this is the method: By the rule of three, with the sine of the true Moon's [longitude]: if with a sine equal to the semi-diameter, the sine of twenty-four degrees of declination is obtained, then with the Moon's sine, what [declination-sine is obtained]? — the sine of the declination degrees is obtained. Then it was stated that the Moon, situated on the ecliptic, moves from the node northward or southward. For determining [the position] up to the node, the node is subtracted from the true Moon; from the sine of that difference, by the rule of three: if with the semi-diameter sine, the sine of the Moon's deflection degrees is obtained, then with this desired sine, what? — the desired deflection-sine is obtained. Of the deflection-sine and the declination-sine, when converted to arcs, if they are in the same direction, their sum [is taken] — since the Moon is beyond the ecliptic. If in different directions, their difference — since the deflection-circle and Moon are near the ecliptic. One should demonstrate [this] correctly on the sphere. The sine of the sum or difference in degrees — that is the interval between the equator and the Moon. The arc-measure is stated in sine-measure.

body.text: kujagurukoṇāḥ ca evam bhaumabṛhaspatiśanaiścarāḥ ca | yathā candraḥ svasmāt pātāt uttareṇa dakṣiṇena vā apakramamaṇḍalasthitaḥ yāti, evam eva kujagurukoṇāḥ | eteṣām vikṣepamaṇḍalāni vikṣepāpakramayogaviśeṣayuktayaḥ candravat pratipattavyāḥ | cakāraḥ etat eva artham samuccinoti |
body.translated_text: 'Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn likewise' — Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. Just as the Moon, situated on the ecliptic, moves from its own node northward or southward — in exactly the same way do Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. Their deflection-circles and the methods involving the sum and difference of deflection and declination should be understood as for the Moon. The particle 'ca' (and) gathers this very meaning.

body.text:
śīghroccena api budhaśukrau | śīghrodbhūtena budhaśukrau pātāt vikṣepamaṇḍalayoḥ bhramataḥ | etayoḥ śīghroccau apakramamaṇḍale pātabhāgapramāṇagatī bhavataḥ | pātabhā[gāt tattatpradeśe] vikṣepamaṇḍale badhnīyāt | [evam tarhi] etayoḥ apakramaparijñānam api śīghroccāt eva | kutaḥ? apakramamaṇḍalāt pātāt vikṣepam bruvatā taduccayoḥ apakramamaṇḍalasthitiḥ pradarśitā bhavati, yataḥ apakramamaṇḍalasthitaḥ vikṣepamaṇḍale pravartate | [te]na
samyak idam avagamyate ã etayoḥ apakramam api śīghroccāt iti | kutaḥ vikṣepasya eva kevalasya? "śīghroccena api budhaśukrau" iti śīghroccāt pātapravṛttāt etayoḥ vikṣepaparijñānam ucyate, nāpamaparijñānam | ataḥ svataḥ e[va e]tayoḥ apakramānayanam śīghroccāt | evam api apakramamaṇḍalasthitau etau vikṣepamaṇḍale pratartate iti eta[t upapa]nnam eva | etat kutaḥ vikṣepaparijñānamātram eva etayoḥ? upāyāntareṇa vikṣiptam punar svataḥ eva apamaṇḍalāt pratiyakṣeṇa
upadiṣṭam, candravikṣepapradarśitam eva arthaviśeṣam sambhāvayati | sarveṣām eva vikṣepaḥ apakramamaṇḍalāt uttareṇa dakṣiṇena ca | [pātāt] cakracaturbhāgāntare yathā uktāḥ [vikṣe]pabhāgāḥ vikṣepāpakramamaṇḍalayoḥ antare yathā avatiṣṭhante tathā pradarśyante | "apamaṇḍalasya candraḥ pātāt yāti" iti etat api gītikāsu upapadiṣṭa[pātānusāreṇa ava]dheyam | śaśī vikṣepamaṇḍalasthitapātāt prabhṛti vikṣepamaṇḍale pravartate, iti etat anuktam na gamyate | "śīghroccena
api budhaśukrau" iti e[tat api] vaktavyam | ataḥ avaśyam etat āryāsūtram vaktavyam || 3 ||
body.translated_text: 'And Mercury and Venus also by their fast apogee': Mercury and Venus revolve on their deflection-circles from the node, [the deflection being] produced by the fast apogee. Their fast apogees move on the ecliptic with the rate equal to the node-degrees. The deflection-circle should be bound at the ecliptic at [the points corresponding to] the node-degrees. Thus, the determination of their declination too is from the fast apogee alone. Why? Because in saying 'deflection from the node on the ecliptic,' the position of their apogees on the ecliptic has been demonstrated — since one situated on the ecliptic enters the deflection-circle. Hence it is properly understood: their declination too [is computed] from the fast apogee. Why only the deflection alone? 'Mercury and Venus also by their fast apogee' — from the fast apogee, the starting-point of the node, the determination of their deflection is stated, not the determination of declination. Hence, the computation of their declination from the fast apogee follows of itself. Even so, these two, being situated on the ecliptic, enter the deflection-circle — this is indeed established. Why is only the determination of deflection [stated] for these two? By another means, what has been deflected is again taught directly from the ecliptic itself; one should infer the specific meaning demonstrated [already for] the Moon's deflection. The deflection of all [planets] is to the north and south of the ecliptic. From the node, at a quarter-circle interval, the deflection-degrees as stated are shown [to lie] within the interval between the deflection-circle and the ecliptic. The [statement] 'the Moon moves from the node of the ecliptic' is also to be understood in accordance with the nodes established in the <s>Gītikās</s>. That the Moon, starting from the node situated on the deflection-circle, revolves on the deflection-circle — this, though unstated, is understood. 'And Mercury and Venus also by their fast apogee' — this too must be stated. Therefore, this <s>āryā</s>-<s>sūtra</s> must necessarily be stated. // 3 //

body.text: grahāṇām kālāṃśāḥ
body.translated_text: The time-degrees of the planets

body.text: grahāṇām udayāstamayaparijñānāya ādityagrahāntarabhāgān āha ã
body.translated_text: In order to know the rising and setting of the planets, he states the degrees of separation from the Sun:

children.text: candraḥ aṃśaiḥ dvādaśabhiḥ avikṣiptaḥ arkāntarasthitaḥ dṛśyaḥ |
children.translated_text: The Moon, at twelve degrees of separation from the Sun, when undeflected, is visible;

children.text: navabhiḥ bhṛguḥ bhṛgoḥ taiḥ dvyadhikaiḥ dvyadhikaiḥ yathā ślakṣṇāḥ ||4||
children.translated_text: Venus at nine; and from Venus, by [adding] two more [each time], [the remaining planets] in order of subtlety. // 4 //

body.text:
candraḥ aṃśaiḥ dvādaśabhiḥ | ayam aṃśaśabdaḥ sāmānyena vibhāgamātravācī | tena "sāmānyacodanāḥ ca viśeṣe avatiṣṭhante" iti aṃśaviśeṣeṣu avasthāpyante | viśeṣaḥ ca kālāṃśatā | ete kālavibhāgāḥ | te kālabhāgāḥ ucyante | "prāṇena eti kalām bham" [gītikāí, 6] iti uktam | tena ucchvāsaprāṇasya liptāsaṃjñātvam | tataḥ prāṇānām saptaśatasya viṃśatyadhikasya [720] dvādaśa bhāgāḥ, ghaṭikādvayam iti arthaḥ | yataḥ ghaṭikādvayasya prāṇāḥ saptaśatāni viṃśatyadhikāni
[720] | athavā sūryāt paścāt prāk vā kālena antaritaḥ grahaḥ yasmāt [dṛśyaḥ tasmāt] kālāṃśatvam | evam kālabhāgaiḥ dvādaśabhiḥ antaritaḥ candraḥ | avikṣiptaḥ, na vikṣiptaḥ avikṣiptaḥ | arkāntarasthitaḥ | arkāt antaram arkāntaram, tasmin arkāṃtare dvādaśakālāṃśa-pramāṇena avikṣiptaḥ vyavasthitaḥ, nabhasi vyapetābhratamasi lakṣyate |
body.translated_text: 'The Moon, at twelve degrees': This word 'degrees' (<s>aṃśa</s>) denotes division in general. Hence, 'general injunctions apply to specifics' — they are applied to specific types of degrees. And the specific type is time-degrees (<s>kālāṃśa</s>). These are time-divisions. They are called time-parts (<s>kālabhāga</s>). It was stated: 'In one <s>prāṇa</s>, the stellar sphere moves one minute' [<s>Gītikā</s> 6]. Hence the breath-<s>prāṇa</s> has the designation of a minute (<s>liptā</s>). Therefore, twelve parts of seven hundred and twenty <s>prāṇas</s> [720] means two <s>ghaṭikās</s>. Since the <s>prāṇas</s> of two <s>ghaṭikās</s> are seven hundred and twenty [720]. Or: a planet separated from the Sun by time, before or after — since it is visible, hence [it is called] 'time-degree.' Thus, the Moon separated by twelve time-degrees. 'Undeflected' — not deflected. 'Situated at a distance from the Sun' — the distance from the Sun is '<s>arkāntara</s>'; at that Sun-distance, being situated undeflected at the measure of twelve time-degrees, it is observed in the sky when clouds and darkness are absent.

body.text: yadā punar asau vikṣiptaḥ ghaṭikādvayāt ūnādhike kāle dṛśyate, yasmāt arkāt uttareṇa vikṣiptaḥ candraḥ golasya uttaronnatatvāt ūne api ghaṭikādvaye kāle dṛśyate, dakṣiṇavikṣiptaḥ ca unnatatvāt golasya dakṣiṇena ghaṭikādvayādhikakāle dṛśyate | tasmāt uktam avikṣiptaḥ iti | tasmāt vikṣepakarmakṛtvā etat antaram ālocyate |
body.translated_text: But when it is deflected, it is visible at a time more or less than two <s>ghaṭikās</s>: since the Moon, deflected northward from the Sun, is visible even at a time less than two <s>ghaṭikās</s> because of the northward elevation of the sphere; and when deflected southward, because of the elevation of the sphere to the south, it is visible at a time more than two <s>ghaṭikās</s>. Therefore it is said 'undeflected.' Therefore, having performed the deflection-correction, this interval is to be considered.

body.text:
navabhiḥ bhṛguḥ | tathā eva kālabhāgaiḥ navabhiḥ arkāntarasthitaḥ avikṣiptaḥ bhṛguḥ dṛśyate | navabhiḥ kālabhāgaiḥ vikṣiptasya vikṣepakarma candravat eva | bhṛgoḥ taiḥ | bhṛgoḥ śukrasya ye bhāgāḥ | navabhiḥ bhṛguḥ taiḥ dvyadhikaiḥ dvyadhikaiḥ iti etāvatā siddhe punar bhṛgugrahaṇam kurvan ācāryaḥ jñāpayati ã bhṛgoḥ iyam kāṣṭhabhāgāḥ nava iti, tebhyaḥ eva navabhyaḥ gurvādyantarabhāgapratipattiḥ | anyathā hi ayam bhṛguḥ ataḥ nyūneṣu api triṣu
caturṣu vā antaritaḥ vakrakāle udayāstamayau kurvan lakṣyate iti etat punar bhṛgugrahaṇam | taiḥ dvyadhikaiḥ dvyadhikaiḥ iti vīpsāgrahaṇam ca bhāgadvayāntaragrahaṇārtham | anyathā hi sarveṣām eva nava eva bhāgāḥ syuḥ |
body.translated_text: 'Venus at nine': Similarly, Venus, at nine time-degrees of separation from the Sun, is visible when undeflected. For Venus with nine time-degrees of deflection, the deflection-correction is exactly as for the Moon. 'From Venus, by those': The degrees that belong to Venus. Since the matter is accomplished by 'Venus at nine, and by those increased by two each time,' the <s>ācārya</s>, by again mentioning Venus, indicates: the arc-degrees of Venus are nine — from those very nine, the degrees of separation of Jupiter and the like are to be understood. For otherwise, this Venus is also observed rising and setting when separated by even fewer [degrees] — three or four — during retrograde. Hence this re-mention of Venus. And the repetition 'increased by two, increased by two' (<s>vīpsā</s>) is for the purpose of indicating a gap of two degrees [each time]. Otherwise, all would have just nine degrees.

body.text: yathā ślakṣṇāḥ | ete grahāḥ ślakṣṇāḥ parihīyamānaśarīrāḥ pratipāditāḥ tathā dvyadhikaiḥ dvyadhikaiḥ arkāntarasthitāḥ avikṣiptāḥ santaḥ dṛśyante | uktaḥ ca eṣām yathāślakṣṇakramaḥ ã
body.translated_text: 'In order of subtlety' (<s>yathā ślakṣṇāḥ</s>): These planets have been presented as subtle, i.e., of diminishing size; accordingly, being at [separations] increased by two each time from the Sun, undeflected, they are visible. And the order of their subtlety has been stated:

body.text: bhṛgugurubudhaśanibhaumāḥ śaśi-ṅa-ña-ṇa-na-māṃśākāḥ | [gītikāí, 7]
body.translated_text: Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, Saturn, Mars — having [apparent] sizes of Moon-<s>ṅa</s>-<s>ña</s>-<s>ṇa</s>-<s>na</s> parts. [<s>Gītikā</s> 7]

body.text:
iti | bhṛgoḥ bhāgaiḥ dvyadhikaiḥ bṛhaspatiḥ dṛśyate ṣaḍbhāgonaghaṭikādvayena, taiḥ dvyadhikaiḥ bṛhaspateḥ trayodaśabhiḥ ṣaḍbhāgottaraghaṭikādvayena budhaḥ, budhabhāgaiḥ dvyadhikaiḥ śanaiścaraḥ sārdhena ghātikādvayena, śanaiścarabhāgaiḥ dvyadhikaiḥ bhaumaḥ ṣaḍbhāgonaghaṭikātrayeṇa, etāvadbhiḥ kālabhāgaiḥ antaritāḥ dṛśyante iti uktam | adarśanam punar eṣām katham avagamyate? kecit tāvat āhuḥ ã etāvadbhiḥ eva bhāgaiḥ | kutaḥ? tulyatā saṃhitāyām
| arkāntarasthitaḥ dṛśyaḥ adṛśyaḥ ca | katham etāvadbhiḥ eva bāgaiḥ dṛśyaḥ adṛśyaḥ ca? yadā arkāt niṣkrāmati grahaḥ tadā tāvadbhiḥ eva dṛśyate, yadā sa eva arkam praviśati tadā [tāvadbhi]ḥ eva antaritaḥ na dṛśyate | etat ca [na] ã yāvatā niṣkrāmataḥ praviśataḥ vā grahasya tulyam idam antaram, tena dṛśyena vā graheṇa bhavitavyam adṛśyena vā | sa tāvat iṣṭakālāṃśakaiḥ dṛśyaḥ eva upalabhyate | tasmāt tulyasaṃhitāvyākhyānam asat iti | katham tarhi? ucyate ã etāvadbhiḥ
eva bhāgaiḥ arkāntarasthitaḥ niṣkrāmat praviśat vā dṛśyate | ūnaiḥ ataḥ dṛśyate iti arthāt avagamyate, adhikaiḥ punar nitarām dṛśyate iti etat aśāstrajñaḥ api jānāti |
body.translated_text: Thus: <s>Bṛhaspati</s> (Jupiter) is visible at [a separation from the Sun] two degrees more than <s>Bhṛgu</s> (Venus), [i.e.,] in two <s>ghaṭikās</s> less one-sixth; at thirteen [degrees], two more than those [of Jupiter], <s>Budha</s> (Mercury) [is visible] in two <s>ghaṭikās</s> plus one-sixth; at [a separation] two degrees more than <s>Budha</s>’s degrees, <s>Śanaiścara</s> (Saturn) [is visible] in two-and-a-half <s>ghaṭikās</s>; at [a separation] two degrees more than <s>Śanaiścara</s>’s degrees, <s>Bhauma</s> (Mars) [is visible] in three <s>ghaṭikās</s> less one-sixth — it is stated that they are visible when separated by these many time-degrees. But how is their invisibility determined? Some say: by those very same degrees. Why? Because of the equality [of setting and rising degrees] as stated in the <s>Saṃhitā</s>. A [planet] situated within the Sun’s [proximity] is either visible or invisible. How can it be visible or invisible at those very same degrees? When a planet exits from the Sun, it is visible at exactly those many [degrees]; when that same [planet] enters the Sun, at exactly those many [degrees] of separation it is invisible. But this is not so — since for a planet either exiting or entering, this interval is equal, therefore the planet must be either [always] visible or [always] invisible [at that distance]. But it is found to be visible at a desired time [with those degrees of separation]. Therefore, the explanation based on equality in the <s>Saṃhitā</s> is incorrect. How then? It is said: at exactly those many degrees of separation from the Sun, [the planet] exiting or entering is visible. At fewer [degrees] than those, it is visible — this is understood from the meaning; and at more [degrees], it is all the more visible — even one ignorant of the <s>śāstra</s> knows this.

body.text:
kālānayanam punar atra deśāntarākṣaviśeṣarāśyudayapramāṇaiḥ parikalpyate | tat yathā ã yadi triṃśatā svadeśarāśyudayakālaḥ labhyate tadā idānīm niṣpannārkagrahāntarabhāgaiḥ kaḥ iti, kālaḥ labhyate | sa yadi abhīṣṭagrahāntarakālena tulyaḥ tadā asau grahaḥ dṛśyate, ūne astam gataḥ, adhike nitarām dṛśyate | athavā svadeśarāśyudayena triṃśatā ca trairāśikam kṛtvā sarvarāśiṣu antarabhāgānayanam ã yadi rāśyudayakālena triṃśadbhāgāḥ labhyante
tadā iṣṭagrahāntarābhihitakālena kiyantaḥ iti sarvarāśiṣu antarabhāgāḥ labhyante | taiḥ vā sakṛtsiddhaiḥ eva antarabhāgaiḥ iṣṭadeśe grahasya darśanam vaktavyam | grahāṇām pūrvodayāstamayayoḥ idam karma | aparodayāstamayayoḥ tatsaptamarāśyudayakālena etat parikalpanam, yasmāt udayarāśivaśāt eva astam rāśayaḥ gacchanti || 4 ||
body.translated_text: The computation of the time [of visibility], moreover, is determined here by the rising-times of the signs at the specific local longitude and latitude. That is: if thirty [degrees] yield the rising-time of the sign at one’s own locality, then by the planet-Sun separation degrees now obtained, what [time is obtained]? — the time is obtained. If that [time] is equal to the specified separation-time of the planet, then that planet is visible; if less, it has set; if more, it is all the more visible. Alternatively, having performed the rule of three with the local sign-rising-time and thirty [degrees], the separation-degrees in all signs [are computed]: if by the sign-rising-time, thirty degrees are obtained, then by the specified planet-separation-time, how many [degrees]? — the separation-degrees in all signs are obtained. With those separation-degrees, determined once and for all, the visibility of the planet at a desired locality is to be stated. This procedure is for the eastern rising and setting of the planets. For the western rising and setting, the computation is made with the rising-time of the seventh sign from that [sign], since the signs set in accordance with the rising sign. || 4 ||

body.text: bhūgrahādīnām prakāśahetuḥ
body.translated_text: The cause of illumination of the Earth, planets, and stars

body.text: dharitrīgrahanakṣatratārāṇām prakāśahetupradarśanāya āha ã
body.translated_text: To demonstrate the cause of illumination of the Earth, planets, <s>nakṣatras</s> (asterisms), and stars, he says:

children.translated_text: The hemispheres of the Earth, planets, and stars are dark due to their own shadow;
the [other] halves shine, facing the Sun, each in proportion [to their size]. || 5 ||

body.text: bhūḥ pṛthivī | grahāḥ sūryādayaḥ | bhāni jyotīṃṣi nakṣatrāṇi | bhūḥ ca grahāḥ ca bhāni ca bhūgrahabhāni, teṣām bhūgrahabhānām | golārdhāni | dharitryādīnām śarīrāṇi golaśabdena ucyante | ataḥ teṣām golānām ardhāni golākāraśarīrārdhāni iti yāvat |
body.translated_text: '<s>Bhū</s>' means the Earth. '<s>Grahas</s>' are the Sun and so forth. '<s>Bhāni</s>' are luminaries, the <s>nakṣatras</s> (asterisms). Earth, planets, and luminaries are '<s>bhūgraha-bhāni</s>'; of those Earth-planets-luminaries. 'Hemispheres' (<s>golārdhāni</s>): the bodies of the Earth and so forth are denoted by the word '<s>gola</s>' (sphere). Therefore, the halves of those spheres — the halves of their spherical bodies — is the meaning.

body.text:
katham ete grahādayaḥ golākāraśarīrāṇi pratipadyante? bhuvam tāvat anye śakaṭākārām darpaṇavṛttākārām ca manyante | na etat evam | yathā golākārā bhūḥ pratipadyate tathā uttarataḥ vakṣyāmi | katham punar atra amī grahāḥ golākārāḥ pratipadyante? atha ca darpaṇavṛttākārau sūryācandramasau lakṣyete, evam anye api | anyat ca ã sthityardhādiparilekhanaprakriyā ca golākāraśarīreṣu na ghaṭate | na etat asti | ete grahādayaḥ golaśarīrāḥ api santaḥ
dūradeśavartitvāt darpaṇavṛttākārāḥ upalakṣyante | yā sthityardhādiparilekhanaprakriyā sā dṛgviṣayā, tasyāḥ dṛgviṣayatvāt yathādarśanagatāni eva bimbasaṃsthānāni aṅgīkṛtya ācāryeṇa uktam | athavā golākāreṣu api sthityardhādyupapattiḥ śakyate vaktum | yasmāt vikṣepādayaḥ bimbamadhyāt pravṛttāḥ tāvat jñātvā golakānām bimbārdham darpaṇavṛttākāraḥ iva yathā bhraman niṣpāditaḥ samudgataḥ tasyāḥ udaram darpaṇavṛttākāram eva upalakṣyate, tasmāt golākārāt
api sthityardhādyupapattisiddhiḥ ca | ataḥ paramārthataḥ eva golākārāḥ, anyathā hi candramasaḥ sitakṣayavṛddhī darpaṇavṛttākāre bimbe na saṃvadete | tasmāt golākāraśarīrāḥ ete | uktam ca ã
body.translated_text: How are these planets and so forth established as having spherical bodies? As for the Earth, some consider it to be cart-shaped or mirror-disc-shaped. This is not so. That the Earth is sphere-shaped, I shall demonstrate later below. But how are these planets established here as sphere-shaped? And yet the Sun and Moon are observed as having mirror-disc shapes, and so are the others. Furthermore, the procedure of delineating the <s>sthityardha</s> (half-duration [of eclipses]) and so forth does not work with spherical bodies. This is not valid. These planets and so forth, even though they have spherical bodies, are perceived as having mirror-disc shapes because they are situated in a distant region. The procedure of delineating the <s>sthityardha</s> and so forth is a matter of observation (<s>dṛgviṣaya</s>); since it pertains to visual observation, the <s>ācārya</s> (<s>Āryabhaṭa</s>) has stated [it] adopting the disc-configurations as they appear to sight. Alternatively, even for sphere-shaped [bodies], the derivation of the <s>sthityardha</s> and so forth can be stated: since the deflections and so forth, being reckoned from the center of the disc, having determined that the half-disc of a sphere, like a mirror-disc, as if produced by rotation, the belly of that [hemisphere] is perceived as having just a mirror-disc shape — therefore, the derivation of the <s>sthityardha</s> and so forth is accomplished even from a sphere-shape. Hence, they are truly sphere-shaped; otherwise, the waxing and waning of the Moon’s bright portion would not be consistent with a mirror-disc-shaped body. Therefore, these have spherical bodies. And it has been stated:

body.text: sūryaḥ agnimayaḥ golaḥ candraḥ ambumayaḥ svabhāvataḥ svacchaḥ | iti |
body.translated_text: The Sun is a sphere made of fire; the Moon is a sphere made of water, by nature transparent.

body.text:
svacchāyayā vivarṇāni | svā cchāyā svacchāyā, tayā svacchāyayā ardhāni eṣām [vivarṇāni aprakāśātmakāni kṛṣṇāni iti arthaḥ, na tataḥ anyatkārāṇa]m asti vaivarṇyasya | yathā ghaṭasya ātapasthasya ekam pārśvam svacchāyayā eva vivarṇam, evam atra api | yā[ni ardhāni] prakāśante tāni sūryābhimukhāni | ardhāni | teṣām golānām ardhāni, yāvanti avaśiṣṭāni svacchāyāvaivarṇyāni vyatiriktāni | yathāsāram | alpānām alpāni, mahatām mahānti | sūryābhimukhāni,
ādityābhimukhāni | dīpyante cakāsanti |
body.translated_text: 'Dark due to their own shadow' (<s>svacchāyayā vivarṇāni</s>): one’s own shadow is '<s>svacchāyā</s>'; by that own-shadow, the halves of these [bodies] are dark — meaning without light, black — and there is no other cause of their darkness. Just as one side of a pot standing in sunlight is dark due to its own shadow, so too here. The halves that shine are those facing the Sun. 'Halves' — of those spheres, the halves: as many as remain, excluding the halves darkened by their own shadow. 'Each in proportion' (<s>yathāsāram</s>): of small [bodies], small [halves]; of large [bodies], large [halves]. 'Facing the Sun' (<s>sūryābhimukhāni</s>) — facing the Sun (<s>Āditya</s>). 'They shine' (<s>dīpyante</s>) — they radiate.

body.text: candrasya sitabhāgaḥ
body.translated_text: The bright portion of the Moon

body.text:
yadi ardhāni grahāṇām sūryābhimukhāni cakāsanti tadā kim iti candramasaḥ ardhabimbam sarvadā na cakāsti? cakāsti eva | kim iti na upalabhyate? ucyate ã amāvāsyāyām candramasaḥ upari ādityaḥ tadā tasya candramasaḥ upari yat bimbārdham tat aśeṣam avabhāsayati | candrasya amāvāsyopalakṣitoparibimbakendrāt yathā yathā paścāt ādityaḥ avalambate tathā tathā bimbakendram api aparataḥ avalambate | tat kendravaśāt candramasaḥ bimbārdham yāvat
eva amāvāsyopalakṣitam bimbaparidhyardhāvadheḥ avalambate tāvat candramasaḥ bimbam asmābhiḥ upalakṣyate | śeṣam uparisthitatvāt na upalakṣyate | sūryābhimukham api savitṛkarā[t chāditam api na dṛśyate] | tasmāt yāvat yāvat candramasaḥ bimbam savitṛbimbāt ślakṣṇam avalambate tāvān svacchaḥ candramasaḥ śuklaḥ upalakṣyate | tena ca amī jyotsnāvitānāvabhāsinaḥ candrakarāḥ | tena tarhi savitṛmarīcayaḥ tu sa[lila]maye svabhāvāt eva [svaccha]candrabimbe
sammūrcchitāḥ naiśam dhvāntam avadhvāṃsayanti, yathā darpaṇe jale vā divasakarāḥ sammūrcchitāḥ santaḥ gṛhāntargatam tamaḥ kṣapayanti |
body.translated_text: If the halves of planets facing the Sun shine, then why does the Moon’s half-disc not always shine? It does indeed shine. Why then is it not perceived? It is said: At new moon (<s>amāvāsyā</s>), the Sun is above the Moon; at that time, the entire upper half-disc of the Moon is illuminated. As the Sun recedes westward from the center of the Moon’s disc observed at new moon, the disc-center also recedes westward correspondingly. According to [the position of] that center, the Moon’s half-disc — to the extent that it descends from [the position of] the disc-circumference half perceived at new moon — to that extent the Moon’s disc is perceived by us. The remainder, being situated above, is not perceived. Even though facing the Sun, [the illuminated part], being covered by the Sun’s rays, is also not visible. Therefore, to the extent that the Moon’s disc gradually descends from the Sun’s disc, that much of the Moon’s bright transparent portion is perceived as the Moon’s <s>śukla</s> (bright phase). And those are the moonbeams illuminating the canopy of moonlight. Therefore, the Sun’s rays, concentrated in the naturally transparent water-made Moon-disc, dispel the nocturnal darkness, just as the Sun’s rays concentrated in a mirror or water dispel the darkness inside a house.

body.text: candraśṛṅgonnatiḥ
body.translated_text: The elevation of the Moon’s horns (<s>candraśṛṅgonnati</s>)

body.text:
anyat ca ã yaḥ yaḥ candrabimbapradeśāḥ savitṛmārge ṛjutvena vyavasthitaḥ sa eva śṛṅgonnatau upalabhyate, na itaraḥ | tathā ca tat jijñāsavaḥ karma kurvanti | tat yathā ã śuklapratipadādiṣu sūryārdhāstamayakālikau sūryācandramasau kṛtvā sūryonacandrotkramajyā gṛhyate | sā yasmāt pratidivasam upacīyamānā, candramasaḥ śuklam upacīyate | utkramajyā ca upacīyamānapramāṇā | tena tayā utkramajyayā trairāśikam ã yadi vyāsārdhatulyayā utkramajyayā
sphuṭacandrabimbārdham upalabhyate, tadā anayā utkramajyayā kiyat iti, tat kālasitamānam labhyate | śuklāṣṭamyāḥ parataḥ yā sitavṛddhiḥ sā kramajyāvaśāt upacīyamānā lakṣyate iti kramajyā gṛhyate | tāḥ kramajyāḥ pūrvopacitavyāsārdhajyāsu prakṣipya trairāśikam kriyate | athavā ã tābhiḥ eva kramajyābhiḥ candrabimbārdhena trairāśikam kṛtvā yat labdham candrabimbārdhe prakṣiptam sitamānam bhavati | śuklapratipadādiṣu yathā candramasaḥ sitamānam vardhate
tathā kṛṣṇapratipatprabhṛtibhyaḥ sitamānam utkrameṇa apacīyate | tena sūryācandramasoḥ viśeṣāt rāśiṣaṭkam apanīya tathā eva karma kriyate |
body.translated_text: Furthermore: whichever portion of the Moon’s disc is situated in a straight line along the Sun’s path, that alone is perceived as the horn-elevation (<s>śṛṅgonnati</s>), not any other. And thus, those who wish to know [this] perform the computation. That is: on the first day of the bright fortnight (<s>śuklapratipad</s>) and so forth, having made the Sun and Moon contemporaneous at [the time of] the Sun’s half-setting, the versed-sine (<s>utkramajyā</s>) of the Sun-subtracted-Moon [arc] is taken. Since that [versed-sine], increasing daily, [corresponds to] the Moon’s bright portion increasing; and the versed-sine is of increasing magnitude; therefore, with that versed-sine the rule of three [is applied]: if with the versed-sine equal to the semi-diameter, the half of the true Moon-disc is obtained, then with this versed-sine, how much? — that measure of the currently illuminated portion is obtained. After the eighth day of the bright fortnight (<s>śuklāṣṭamī</s>), the increase of the bright portion is observed as growing by means of the [ordinary] sine (<s>kramajyā</s>), so the sine is taken. Those sines, added to the previously accumulated semi-diameter sines, the rule of three is performed. Alternatively: with those very sines, having performed the rule of three with the Moon’s half-disc, whatever is obtained, added to the Moon’s half-disc, becomes the bright measure. Just as from the first day of the bright fortnight onwards the Moon’s bright measure increases, so from the first day of the dark fortnight (<s>kṛṣṇapratipat</s>) onwards, the bright measure decreases in reverse order. Therefore, subtracting six signs from the Sun-Moon difference, the same computation is performed.

body.text: candrasya darśanakālaḥ
body.translated_text: The time of visibility of the Moon

body.text:
darśanakālaḥ hi yāvantam kālam candraḥ dṛśyate | yavatā kālena udeti tat ānayanopāyaḥ ã śuklapakṣe tāvat udayarāśivaśāt eva jyotiścakragatiḥ iti ataḥ yāvantaḥ sūryāt candrarāśibhāgāḥ tāvantaḥ eva udayāvadheḥ svadeśarāśyudayaprāṇāḥ parigṛhyante | tat yathā ã āstamayike savitari ṣaḍrāśayaḥ parikṣipyante sa sūryāt saptamaḥ rāśiḥ bhavati | tathā ca candramasi ṣaḍrāśayaḥ parikṣipya sūryagatarāśibhāgān triṃśatā viśodhayet śeṣam sūryasya āgatarāśibhāgaḥ
| tat ṣaḍrāśiyutasūryavartamānarāśyudayena saṅguṇayya triṃśatā vibhajet, labdham prāṇāḥ | tān ekataḥ vinyaset | sūryāgatarāśibhāgān ca ṣaḍrāśiyutasūrye prakṣipya tāvat svadeśarāśyudayaprāṇāḥ saṃkalanīyāḥ yāvat ṣaḍrāśiyutacandragatāḥ bhāgāḥ | tataḥ ṣaḍrāśiyutacandragatāḥ bhāgāḥ tat rāśyudayaprāṇaiḥ saṅguṇya triṃśatā vibhajet, labdham prāṇāḥ | tān pūrvasaṅkalitaprāṇān ca sarvān ekatra nyastaprāṇeṣu prakṣipya ṣaḍbhiḥ bhāgaḥ, labdham vighaṭikāḥ, ṣaṣṭyā
ghaṭikāḥ | evam ghaṭikādilakṣaṇaḥ darśanakālaḥ | tāvatā kālena sūryācandramasoḥ gativiśeṣaḥ asti iti aviśeṣakarma pravartate | tat yathā ã yadi ṣaṣṭyā ghaṭikābhiḥ sūryabhuktiḥ candrabhuktiḥ vā labhyate tataḥ anena darśanakālena te kiyatyau tayoḥ bhuktī iti | sūryabhuktilabdham ṣaḍrāśiyuktasūrye prakṣipet, candrabhuktilabdham api ṣaḍrāśiyutacandramasi prakṣipya tāvat idam kuryāt yāvat aviśeṣaḥ | tatra yaḥ aviśiṣṭaḥ kālaḥ sa darśanakālaḥ | tāvantam kālam śarvaryām
śaśī dṛśyate | yaḥ ca ṣaḍrāśiyuktaḥ candraḥ aviśiṣṭaḥ tasmāt cakrārdham apanayet tāvān candraḥ darśanakālaparisamāptau astam eti |
body.translated_text: The time of visibility [of the Moon] is the duration for which the Moon is visible. The method for deriving how much time [elapses before] it rises: In the bright fortnight, since the motion of the stellar circle is in accordance with the rising sign, therefore, as many sign-degrees [as there are] of the Moon from the Sun, that many local sign-rising <s>prāṇas</s> (breaths = time-units) are taken from [the time of] rising. That is: to the Sun at the [time of] setting, six signs are added — that becomes the seventh sign from the Sun. Similarly, adding six signs to the Moon and subtracting the Sun’s elapsed sign-degrees from thirty, the remainder is the Sun’s upcoming sign-degrees. Those, multiplied by the rising-time of the current sign of the Sun plus six signs, and divided by thirty, yield <s>prāṇas</s>. Set those aside. Then, adding the Sun’s upcoming sign-degrees to the Sun plus six signs, the local sign-rising <s>prāṇas</s> are accumulated until [the total reaches] the Moon-plus-six-signs elapsed degrees. Then, the Moon-plus-six-signs elapsed degrees, multiplied by that sign’s rising <s>prāṇas</s> and divided by thirty, yield <s>prāṇas</s>. Adding those and the previously accumulated <s>prāṇas</s> all together with the set-aside <s>prāṇas</s>, dividing by six gives <s>vighaṭikās</s>, and by sixty gives <s>ghaṭikās</s>. Thus the visibility-time is in <s>ghaṭikās</s> and so forth. During that time there is a difference in the motions of the Sun and Moon, so the iterative equalization (<s>aviśeṣakarma</s>) is applied. That is: if by sixty <s>ghaṭikās</s>, the Sun’s daily motion or the Moon’s daily motion is obtained, then by this visibility-time, what are their respective motions? The Sun-motion result is added to the Sun plus six signs; the Moon-motion result is also added to the Moon plus six signs; and this [procedure] should be repeated until there is no difference. The time at which there is no difference — that is the visibility-time. For that duration of the night, the Moon is visible. And the Moon plus six signs at the point of no-difference — subtracting half a circle from it gives the Moon [position] at the conclusion of the visibility-time when it sets.

body.text:
atha kaścit yadi kiyatā kālena a[na]stamite savitari candrodayaḥ bhaviṣyati iti etat jijñāsuḥ, idam karma kuryāt | tat yathā ã avikṛtāstamayakālādityabhāgebhyaḥ prabhṛti tāvat prāṇāḥ saṃkalanīyāḥ yāvat avikṛtaśītāṃśoḥ gatabhāgaprāṇāḥ | tān pūrvavat ghaṭikāḥ kṛtvā [dina]pramāṇaghaṭikābhyaḥ viśodhayet | tatra yaḥ śeṣaḥ sa divasaśeṣaḥ | tāvatā divasaśeṣeṇa tadā candrodayaḥ bhaviṣyati | atra api sūryācandramasoḥ aviśeṣakarma pravartate | tat yathā ã āsām
nāḍīnām yaḥ yaḥ bhogaḥ tena adhikau sūryācandramasau iti ataḥ tābhyām apanīya apanīya aviśeṣaḥ kriyate | aviśeṣitaḥ darśanakālaḥ tāvatā kālena divasaśeṣaḥ eva candrodayaḥ | yaḥ asau aviśiṣṭaḥ candraḥ tāvān tatra divasaśeṣodayakāle candraḥ |
body.translated_text: Now, if someone wishes to know after how much time after sunset the Moon will rise, he should perform this procedure. Namely: Starting from the degrees of the Sun at the uncorrected time of sunset, as many <s>prāṇas</s> (breath-units) should be accumulated until the <s>prāṇas</s> corresponding to the traversed degrees of the uncorrected Moon [are reached]. Converting those into <s>ghaṭikās</s> (time-units) as before, one should subtract from the day-measure <s>ghaṭikās</s>. The remainder there is the day-remainder (<s>divasaśeṣa</s>). After that much day-remainder, the moonrise will occur then. Here too, the iteration procedure (<s>aviśeṣakarma</s>) for the Sun and Moon applies. Namely: whatever the traversal-rate of these <s>nāḍīs</s>, by that much the Sun and Moon are in excess; therefore, subtracting repeatedly from both, the iteration is performed. The iterated [value] is the time of visibility; after that much time, the day-remainder is the moonrise. That iterated Moon — that much is the Moon at the time of day-remainder moonrise.

body.text:
athavā prathamānītadivasaśeṣacandrodayakālena candramasaḥ bhuktim saṅguṇayya ṣaṣṭyā vibhajet | labdham candrāt viśodhayet | sa tāvat divasaśeṣakālikaḥ candraḥ bhavati | tataḥ prathamānītadivasakālena udayalagnam kuryāt | tat udayalagnam tena divasaśeṣoditacandreṇa tulyam yadā, tadā divasaśeṣam candrodayakālaḥ | atha yadi tasmāt lagnāt ūnaḥ candraḥ tadā prathamataram uditaḥ iti | tayoḥ lagnacandrayoḥ antarālaprāṇān prathamānītadivasaśeṣakālāt
viśodhayet | teṣām ca prāṇānām yāvatī candrabhuktiḥ trairāśikena labhyate tāvatī prathamadivasaśeṣoditakālacandrāt viśodhyate tāvān candraḥ divasaśeṣoditaḥ, tāvān ca divasaśeṣakālaḥ | candraḥ ca yadā adhikaḥ tadā pūrvavat tadantaraprāṇān divasaśeṣakāle prakṣipet tāvatām prāṇānām candrabhogam candramasi prakṣipet, tāvat karma yāvat aviśeṣaḥ | athavā prathamāstamayikacandrāt eva antarotpannadivasaśeṣakālabhogaḥ candramasaḥ viśodhya tat kālalagnakrameṇa
aviśeṣakarma kriyate |
body.translated_text: Alternatively, multiplying the Moon's daily motion by the initially-derived day-remainder moonrise time, and dividing by sixty — the quotient is subtracted from the Moon. That then becomes the Moon at the time of the day-remainder. Then, with the initially-derived day-time, one should compute the rising ascendant (<s>udayalagna</s>). When that rising ascendant equals the Moon risen at the day-remainder, then the day-remainder is the moonrise time. Now, if the Moon is less than that ascendant, then it has risen earlier. The interval-<s>prāṇas</s> between the ascendant and the Moon should be subtracted from the initially-derived day-remainder time. And the Moon's motion corresponding to those <s>prāṇas</s>, obtained by the rule of three, is subtracted from the Moon at the initially-derived day-remainder rising time — that much is the Moon risen at the day-remainder, and that much is the day-remainder time. When, however, the Moon exceeds [the ascendant], then as before, those interval-<s>prāṇas</s> should be added to the day-remainder time, and the Moon's traversal corresponding to those <s>prāṇas</s> should be added to the Moon — [repeating] this operation until iteration [converges]. Alternatively, from the Moon at the initial sunset itself, subtracting the Moon's traversal produced during the interval day-remainder time, the iteration procedure is performed in the ascendant-time sequence.

body.text:
atha yadi udayalagnāt candraḥ adhikaḥ tadā [kiyan]nāḍyā abhyudeti candraḥ iti tadantaraprāṇān prathamānītadivasaśeṣe prakṣipet | tat bhuktim candramasi prakṣipet tāvat yāvat aviśeṣaḥ | evam udayalagnam candraḥ ca kṛtaḥ bhavati, divasaśeṣacandrodayakālaḥ ca | evam yāvat paurṇamāsī tāvat darśanakālānayanam | paurṇamāsyām punar tāvat eva antaraghaṭikāḥ yadi dinapramāṇaghaṭikābhyaḥ ūnāḥ bhaveyuḥ tadā anastamite āditye candrodayaḥ, yadi atiriktāḥ
tadā astaṃgate | ubhayatra api antarakālapramāṇena aviśeṣakarma anantarakarmavat eva | kṛṣṇapakṣapratipadādiṣu ca candrādityāntaraghaṭikābhyaḥ dinapramāṇaghaṭikāḥ viśodhya śeṣa[ghaṭikā]bhiḥ bhukiḥ trairāśikena sūryācandramasau sañcārya punar tayoḥ antaraghaṭikābhyaḥ dinapramāṇaghaṭikāḥ viśodhayet | śeṣaghaṭikābhiḥ candrādityau tadantarālaghaṭikāḥ iti ādyaviśeṣāntam karma kriyate, tatra aviśiṣṭena kālena [sūryāstamayāt paścāt candrodayaḥ | evam
eva aviśiṣṭena kālena] sūryodayāt prāk candrodayaḥ |
body.translated_text: Now, if the Moon exceeds the rising ascendant, then [the question is:] after how many <s>nāḍīs</s> does the Moon rise? Those interval-<s>prāṇas</s> should be added to the initially-derived day-remainder. That [Moon's] motion should be added to the Moon — [repeating] until iteration [converges]. Thus the rising ascendant and the Moon are determined, and the day-remainder moonrise time [is established]. In this manner, the computation of the time of visibility [proceeds] up to the full-moon day (<s>paurṇamāsī</s>). On the full-moon day, if the interval-<s>ghaṭikās</s> are less than the day-measure <s>ghaṭikās</s>, then the moonrise [occurs] before sunset; if they exceed [the day-measure], then after sunset. In both cases, the iteration procedure with the interval-time measure [is the same] as the immediately preceding procedure. And on the first day of the dark fortnight (<s>kṛṣṇapakṣa</s>) onward, subtracting the day-measure <s>ghaṭikās</s> from the Moon-Sun interval-<s>ghaṭikās</s>, with the remaining <s>ghaṭikās</s> the motion is obtained by the rule of three, the Sun and Moon are advanced, then again from the interval-<s>ghaṭikās</s> of those two, the day-measure <s>ghaṭikās</s> are subtracted. With the remaining <s>ghaṭikās</s>, the Moon and Sun [are advanced] for those interval-<s>ghaṭikās</s> — the operation is performed until the first iteration [converges]; by the iterated time, [the day-remainder gives] the moonrise after sunset. In exactly the same way, by the iterated time, [one obtains] the moonrise before sunrise.

body.text:
atha anastamite savitari kiyatā kālena candraḥ astam yāsyati iti etat jijñāsuḥ idam karma kuryāt | tat yathā ã sūryodayakālotpannam candramasam kṛtvā tatra rāśiṣaṭkam prakṣipet | [tataḥ] prāk candrodayaḥ [jñātavyaḥ] | atha audayikāt ādityāt ṣaḍrāśiyuktaniśākarāvadheḥ svadeśarāśyudayavidhānena yāvatyaḥ ghaṭikāḥ tāḥ aviśeṣyante | katham? tāsām trairāśikena yāvat candramasaḥ bhuktiḥ tām candramasi prakṣipet iti ataḥ punar api tasmāt ādityāt
ṣaḍrāśiyuktacandrāvadheḥ pūrvavat ghaṭikāḥ tāvat yāvat aviśeṣaḥ | tatra yāḥ aviśeṣitāḥ ghaṭikāḥ tāvatībhiḥ divase vyatītābhiḥ candraḥ astam eti | divasapramāṇāt viśodhya śeṣam dinaśeṣaghaṭikāḥ ca | atra yaḥ aviśiṣṭaḥ candraḥ sa tasmin kāle tāvān, yaḥ ca ṣaḍrāśiyuktaḥ candraḥ sa tasmin kāle udayalagnam iti |
body.translated_text: Now, if someone wishes to know after how much time before sunset the Moon will set, he should perform this procedure. Namely: Having computed the Moon at the time of sunrise, one should add six signs to it. [From this,] the prior moonrise [is to be known]. Then, from the rising Sun to the Moon augmented by six signs, however many <s>ghaṭikās</s> [are obtained] by the rising-time method of one's locality, those are iterated. How? The Moon's motion corresponding to those [<s>ghaṭikās</s>], obtained by the rule of three, is added to the Moon; therefore, again from that Sun to the Moon augmented by six signs, <s>ghaṭikās</s> [are computed] as before — [repeating] until iteration [converges]. There, the iterated <s>ghaṭikās</s> — after that many elapsed [<s>ghaṭikās</s>] in the day, the Moon sets. Subtracting from the day-measure, the remainder is the day-remainder <s>ghaṭikās</s>. Here, the iterated Moon is the Moon at that time, and the Moon augmented by six signs — that is the rising ascendant at that time.

body.text: candrasya yāmyottarapradeśaḥ
body.translated_text: The Moon's southern and northern position

body.text:
atha kaścit kiyatā kālena śuklāṣṭamyā parataḥ candraḥ gaganamadhyam avagāhate, kiyān vā tatra candraḥ iti jijñāsuḥ, idam karma kuryāt | atha tatkālāt parataḥ svadhiyā āsannau madhyalagnaniśākarau abhyūhya, tatra yadi madhyalagnaniśākarau tulyau syātām tadā tāvān candraḥ tāvatā eva kālena gaganamadhyam ārokṣyati | atha yadi adhikaḥ candraḥ tadā na adya api prāpnoti gaganamadhyam | tatra madhyalagnacandrāntarakālam svadhiyā abhyūhitakāle
prakṣipya madhyalagnacandrau kuryāt yāvat tulyau iti | atha madhyalagnāt ūnaḥ candraḥ tadā tadantarālakālam svadhiyā abhyūhita[kālāt viśodhya] madhyalagnacandrau tāvat kuryāt yāvat madhyalagnacandrau tulyau syātām | evam prasādhitagaganamadhyādhirūḍhāmṛtadīdhiteḥ apakramavikṣepākṣaiḥ madhyacchāyā prasādhyate |
body.translated_text: Now, if someone wishes to know after how much time after the eighth day of the bright fortnight the Moon enters the mid-heaven (<s>gaganamadhya</s>), and what the Moon's [longitude] is at that time, he should perform this procedure. Then, from that time onward, having estimated by one's own intelligence the approximate meridian-ascendant (<s>madhyalagna</s>) and Moon, if the meridian-ascendant and Moon are equal, then that much is the Moon and at that very time [the Moon] will ascend to the mid-heaven. But if the Moon exceeds [the meridian-ascendant], then it has not yet reached the mid-heaven today. In that case, adding the meridian-ascendant-Moon interval-time to the estimated time by one's own intelligence, one should compute the meridian-ascendant and Moon until they are equal. But if the Moon is less than the meridian-ascendant, then subtracting that interval-time from the time estimated by one's own intelligence, one should compute the meridian-ascendant and Moon until the meridian-ascendant and Moon are equal. Having thus determined [the time when] the Moon ascends to the mid-heaven, the meridian shadow (<s>madhyacchāyā</s>) is computed using the declination, deflection, and latitude.

body.text: candraśṛṅgonnatiparilekhanavidhiḥJ
body.translated_text: Procedure for drawing the lunar crescent elevation (<s>candraśṛṅgonnati</s>)

body.text:
atha candrāgrācandraśaṅkvagrayoḥ tulyadikkayoḥ yogaḥ, bhinnadikkayoḥ viśeṣaḥ, tat yogaviśeṣatulyam iṣṭakāle [bāhu]ḥ candramasaḥ | sa ca antarālataḥ sūryāgrayā saha ekadikkam viśeṣyate, yataḥ arkāt eva uttareṇa dakṣiṇena vā candraḥ sādhyate, na viṣuvataḥ | vidikkayoḥ yojyate yasmāt yogaḥ arkacandrāntaram | etat chedyake gole vā pradarśyam | evam pariniṣṭhitapramāṇam bhujā sūryāt yāmya uttarāyatā prasāryate | candraśaṅkuḥ koṭiḥ | sa yadi sūryāt
uttareṇa candraḥ tadā bhujottarāgrataḥ pūrvāparāyatā prasāryate | yadā dakṣiṇena candraḥ sūryāt tadā tasyāḥ bhujāyāḥ dakṣiṇāgrataḥ pūrvāparāyatā | evam bhujakoṭī yathāgatapramāṇena vinyasya bhujākoṭimastakāvagāhī karṇaḥ dūranirgatāgraḥ prasārya koṭyagrakarṇasampāte kendram viracya candrabimbam ālikhet | tasya candrabimbaparidheḥ aparataḥ karṇānusāreṇa sitamānam nītvā bindum kuryāt | candrabimbakendrapūrvāpare karṇaḥ, tat matsyavidhānāt dakṣiṇottare
sādhye | dakṣiṇottararekhācandraparidhisampāte bindū kriyete | tataḥ tābhyām pūrvavihitabindunā ca tathā chedyakavidhānena tat bindutrayaśiraḥspṛgvṛttam ālikhet | tasya vṛttasya candrabimbaparidheḥ ca yat antaram tat candramasaḥ śuklaḥ | atha eva śrṅgonnatiḥ nabhasi upalakṣyate |
body.translated_text: Now, when the Moon's <s>agrā</s> (amplitude) and the Moon's gnomon-shadow (<s>śaṅkvagra</s>) are in the same direction, their sum [is taken]; when in different directions, their difference. That sum or difference, at the desired time, equals the <s>bāhu</s> (base) of the Moon. And that is combined with or differenced from the Sun's <s>agrā</s> (amplitude) — in the same direction, the difference [is taken], since the Moon is determined to the north or south of the Sun, not from the equator; in different directions, the sum [is taken], since the sum is the Sun-Moon interval. This should be demonstrated on the projection diagram or the [armillary] sphere. Thus, the base of the determined measure is extended from the Sun southward or northward. The Moon's gnomon (<s>candraśaṅku</s>) is the perpendicular (<s>koṭi</s>). If the Moon is to the north of the Sun, then from the northern end of the base, [the perpendicular] is extended east-west. When the Moon is to the south of the Sun, then from the southern end of that base, [the perpendicular is extended] east-west. Having thus set down the base and perpendicular with their determined measures, a hypotenuse (<s>karṇa</s>) spanning the tips of base and perpendicular, with its end extending far out, is drawn. At the intersection of the perpendicular-end and hypotenuse, a center is made and the Moon's disc is drawn. From the western part of that Moon-disc circumference, the bright measure (<s>sitamāna</s>) is carried along the direction of the hypotenuse, and a point is made. On the east-west [line] through the Moon-disc center, [lies] the hypotenuse; by the fish-figure method, the north-south [line] is determined. At the intersections of the north-south line and the Moon's circumference, two points are made. Then, with those two [points] and the previously established point, by the projection-diagram method, a circle passing through those three points is drawn. The [area] between that circle and the Moon-disc circumference is the bright portion (<s>śukla</s>) of the Moon. Thus the crescent elevation (<s>śṛṅgonnati</s>) is observed in the sky.

body.text:
śuklāṣṭamyāḥ parataḥ astakālodayalagnāgrajyayā arkāgrāvat karma [kriyate] | candrodayalagnāntaraprāṇotpannaḥ śaṅkuḥ, koṭiḥ aparābhimukhī tathā eva prasāryate | tatra yathāgatam sitamānam candrabimbapramāṇāt viśodhyam śeṣam asitam bhavati | tatkarṇānusāreṇa candraparidhipūrvabhāgāt bimbāntare asitamānam nītvā bindum kuryāt | tena dakṣiṇottarabindubhyām ca pūrvavat bindutrayaśiraḥspṛgvṛttam ālikhet | tasya candrabimbaparidheḥ ca yat
antaram tat asitam | kṛṣṇapratipadādiṣu ca aparābhimukhaprasāritakoṭikarṇāgralikhitacandraparidhyaparabhāgāt karṇānusāreṇa asitam antaḥ pūrvavat vṛttam ālikhet | iṣṭakāle tu yathā pratyāsannāstodayalagnajyām arkāgrām parikalpya tatkālacandraśaṅkvagram āpādya iṣṭalagnacandrāntaraprāṇotpannaśaṅkukoṭyā candraḥ parilekhanīyaḥ | evam sarvatra kṣitijāt upari vyavasthitasya candrasya parilekhanaprakriyā |
body.translated_text: After the eighth [day] of the bright fortnight, the operation is performed with the <s>agrā</s>-sine of the setting-time rising-ascendant as if it were the Sun's <s>agrā</s>. The gnomon produced from the Moon-rising-ascendant interval-<s>prāṇas</s> is the perpendicular, [which is] extended westward in the same manner. There, the bright measure as determined is subtracted from the Moon-disc measure; the remainder is the dark portion (<s>asita</s>). Along the direction of that hypotenuse, from the eastern part of the Moon's circumference, the dark measure is carried into the disc's interior and a point is made. With that and the north-south points, as before, a circle passing through those three points is drawn. The [area] between that [circle] and the Moon-disc circumference is the dark portion. And on the first day of the dark fortnight and afterward, with the perpendicular and hypotenuse-end drawn westward, a circle is drawn as before inside [the disc] from the western part of the Moon's circumference, along the direction of the hypotenuse, marking the dark [portion] inward. At a desired time, however, having postulated the <s>agrā</s>-sine of the ascendant closest to setting or rising as the Sun's <s>agrā</s>, having derived the Moon's gnomon-<s>agra</s> at that time, [and] with the gnomon-perpendicular produced from the desired-ascendant-Moon interval-<s>prāṇas</s>, the Moon should be drawn. In this manner, everywhere, the procedure for drawing the Moon situated above the horizon [is given].

body.text: gṛhapaṭalam vidārya śṛṅgonnatidarśanam
body.translated_text: Observing the crescent elevation through a house-roof opening

body.text:
atha śaṅkubhujākoṭikarṇapramāṇaparikalpitayantrāgre gṛhapaṭalabimbāntare śiśiradīdhitigaṇitasitapramāṇaśṛṅgonnatiḥ pradṛśyate | tat yathā ã samyak prasiddhagṛhodare pūrvāpararekhātaḥ uttareṇa dakṣiṇena vā parikalpitāṅgulapramāṇam arkāgrāsūtram pūrvavat prasārya bindum kuryāt | saḥ arkabinduḥ | pūrvāpararekhāyāḥ eva dakṣiṇottarataḥ candrāgrataḥ śaṅkvagrayoḥ yogaviśeṣajyāṅgulatulyam sūtram yathā āgatadiśam prasārya bindum kuryāt
| sa śaśibinduḥ | arkendubindvoḥ antarāṅgulatulyā bhujā | tatkāla[candra]śaṅkutulyā koṭiḥ avalambakaḥ | tadanusāreṇa avalambakasthityā candrabimbānusāriṇyā gṛhapaṭalam vidārayet | tatra śaṅkvagrāyatadaṇḍaśirasi yathālikhitam tat chedyakasitaśṛṅgonnatim arkabindunyastadṛṣṭiḥ karṇānusāreṇa utkṣiptāvalambakāṅgulapramāṇamastakāsaktam śaśalakṣmāṇam paśyati | evam eva grahāḥ api gṛhodaravyavasthitaiḥ darśanīyāḥ iti |
body.translated_text: Now, with an instrument whose tip is calibrated to the measure of the gnomon, base, perpendicular, and hypotenuse, within a house-roof opening, the lunar crescent elevation computed by the calculated bright measure is displayed. Namely: In a well-known, properly-oriented house-interior, from the east-west line, to the north or south, a thread of calibrated <s>aṅgula</s>-measure equal to the Sun's <s>agrā</s> is extended as before and a point is made. That is the Sun-point. From the east-west line itself, to the south or north, from the Moon's <s>agrā</s> — a thread equal in <s>aṅgula</s>-measure to the sum or difference of the [Moon's] gnomon-shadow [and amplitude] — is extended in the appropriate direction and a point is made. That is the Moon-point. The interval in <s>aṅgulas</s> between the Sun-point and Moon-point is the base. The perpendicular — equal to the Moon's gnomon at that time — is the plumb-line (<s>avalambaka</s>). Following that, with a plumb-line stand following the Moon-disc, the house-roof is pierced. There, on the tip of a rod extended along the gnomon-shadow, the projection-diagram crescent-elevation as previously drawn — with the gaze fixed on the Sun-point, along the direction of the hypotenuse, with the plumb-line of the <s>aṅgula</s>-measure raised aloft and attached at the tip — one sees the Moon (<s>śaśalakṣman</s>). In exactly this way, the planets too should be observed by those situated within the house-interior.

body.text: ardhodite candre śṛṅgonnatikalpanā
body.translated_text: Crescent elevation when the Moon is half-risen

body.text:
kṣitijamaṇḍalākrāntārdhabimbasya candramasaḥ koṭeḥ abhāvāt na parilikhyate | tatra udayāstajyācandrāgre śṛṅgasya unnatiḥ parikalpyate | tat yathā ã yadi candrāgrā dakṣiṇena udayajyā uttareṇa tadā candramasaḥ uttaraśṛṅgam prāk pradṛśyate, yataḥ bhavṛttacandraḥ dakṣiṇena vyavasthitaḥ | bhavṛttacandrānusāreṇa ca sūryamarīcayaḥ candrabimbam karṇagatyā avagāhante | yadā punar candrāgrā uttareṇa udayajyā dakṣiṇena tadā candramasaḥ dakṣiṇaśṛṅgam
prāk pradṛśyate | yasmāt candramasaḥ dakṣiṇena bhavṛttaḥ sthitaḥ | bhavṛttānusāreṇa ca sūryamarīcayaḥ candrabimbam avagāhante | dakṣiṇena tulyadikkayoḥ viśeṣaḥ, candrāgrā yadā atiricyate tadā candramasaḥ uttaraśṛṅgam prāk pradṛśyate, anyathā dakṣiṇam | uttareṇa yadā candrāgrā atiricyate tadā dakṣiṇaśṛṅgam prāk pradṛśyate, anyathā uttaram | yadā punar viśeṣeṇa na kiñcit antaram tadā yugapat ubhayaśṛṅgadarśanam | yadā ca udayajyā candrāgre na bhavataḥ
tadā ca astamaye candramasaḥ astalagnajyayā candrāgrayā ca śṛṅgasya prāk paścāt vā astamayam parikalpanīyam |
body.translated_text: The <s>koṭi</s> (perpendicular) of the Moon whose half-disc is overlapped by the horizon circle is not drawn, due to its absence. There, the elevation of the crescent horn is to be determined from the <s>udayāstajyā</s> (rising-setting sine) and the <s>candrāgrā</s> (lunar amplitude). That is as follows: if the <s>candrāgrā</s> is to the south and the <s>udayajyā</s> (rising sine) is to the north, then the northern horn of the Moon is seen first, because the Sun on the ecliptic is situated to the south of the Moon. Following the Sun on the ecliptic, the rays of the Sun penetrate the Moon's disc diagonally. When, however, the <s>candrāgrā</s> is to the north and the <s>udayajyā</s> is to the south, then the southern horn of the Moon is seen first, because the ecliptic is situated to the south of the Moon. Following the ecliptic, the rays of the Sun penetrate the Moon's disc. When both are in the same direction to the south, whichever exceeds — if the <s>candrāgrā</s> exceeds, then the northern horn of the Moon is seen first, otherwise the southern. When the <s>candrāgrā</s> exceeds to the north, then the southern horn is seen first, otherwise the northern. When there is no difference whatsoever in the remainder, then both horns are seen simultaneously. And when there is no <s>udayajyā</s> or <s>candrāgrā</s>, then at the time of setting, the rising or setting of the crescent horn is to be determined from the <s>astalagnajyā</s> (setting-point sine) and the <s>candrāgrā</s>, whether eastward or westward.

body.text: candrasya sitāsitahetuḥ
body.translated_text: The cause of the bright and dark parts of the Moon

body.text: evam candramasaḥ sitāsitaśṛṅgonnatidarśanakālādayaḥ savitṛvaśāt eva | evam ca nirukte paṭhyate ã
body.translated_text: Thus, the bright and dark parts, the elevation of the crescent horns, the time of visibility, and so forth of the Moon are entirely dependent on the Sun. And thus it is read in the <s>Nirukta</s>:

body.text: tasya ekau raśmiḥ candramasam prati dīpyate |
body.translated_text: One ray of his shines towards the Moon.

body.text: na hi tena upekṣitavyam | ādityataḥ asya dīptiḥ bhavati |
body.translated_text: This should not be disregarded by anyone. Its brilliance comes from the Sun.

body.text: suṣumṇaḥ sūryaraśmicandramāḥ gandharvaḥ |
body.translated_text: <s>Suṣumṇa</s> is the solar ray; the Moon is a <s>Gandharva</s>.

body.text: vājasaneyasaṃhitā, aí 18, maṃí 40; taittirīyasaṃhitā, 3.4.7.1
body.translated_text: <s>Vājasaneyasaṃhitā</s>, chapter 18, mantra 40; <s>Taittirīyasaṃhitā</s>, 3.4.7.1

body.text:
iti api ca nigamaḥ bhavati iti | tasmāt etena eva liṅgena candramārgāt upari sūryamārgaḥ iti, anyathā anupapatyā | pariśiṣṭāḥ ca tārāgrahāḥ sūryamārgāt upari dūreṇa vyavasthitāḥ | tena teṣām ārātsthitāni golārdhāni sarvadā sakalāni eva cakāsate | ūrdhvamukhāḥ sūryamarīcayaḥ sadā ārādbhāgam prakāśayanti iti | budhaśukrayoḥ ca pratyāsannavartitvāt sarvataḥ bimbam avagāhante arkamarīcayaḥ pradīpapratyāsannagolavat tena tayoḥ api asakalabimbatābhāvaḥ | yadi
evam astamite savitari katham ete grahādayaḥ cakāsate savitṛkarābhāvāt ? na eṣaḥ doṣaḥ | bhūmeḥ dūreṇa sūryamārgaḥ | tena uparimukhānām sūryamarīcīnām na vyavadhānāya bhūḥ vartate | yathā ghaṭasya upari adhaḥ dūreṇa avasthitasya pradīpasya ghaṭaḥ na vyavadhānakāraṇam | kṛṣṇapakṣapratipadādiṣu candramasaḥ bimbapūrvabhāgaḥ pratyāsannaḥ savituḥ iti tena tat śuklam upalabhyate | ratnānām ca ādityakarāḥ eva dīptikāraṇatvam prapadyate | tena tāni
api rātrau na prakāśātmakāni | uktam ca ratnaparīkṣāyām ã
body.translated_text: Thus, there is also a Vedic passage confirming this. Therefore, by this very evidence, the path of the Sun is above the path of the Moon — otherwise it would be logically impossible. And the remaining <s>tārāgrahas</s> (star-planets) are situated far above the path of the Sun. Therefore, the hemispheres of those that are facing nearby always shine fully. The rays of the Sun, directed upward, always illuminate the near side. And because <s>Budha</s> (Mercury) and <s>Śukra</s> (Venus) move in close proximity, the rays of the Sun penetrate their discs from all sides, like a globe placed near a lamp; therefore there is no incomplete disc for those two either. If this is so, then how do these planets and others shine when the Sun has set, since the Sun's rays are absent? This is no defect. The Sun's path is far from the Earth. Therefore, the Earth does not serve as an obstruction for the upward-directed rays of the Sun. Just as a pot is not an obstruction for a lamp placed far above and below it. In the first day of the dark fortnight and so on, the front portion of the Moon's disc is near the Sun, and therefore that part appears bright. And for gems too, the rays of the Sun alone are accepted as the cause of brilliance. Therefore those gems also do not shine at night. And it is stated in the <s>Ratnaparīkṣā</s> (Examination of Gems):

children.text: bhānoḥ ca bhāsām anuvedhayogam āsādya raśmiprakareṇa dūram |
children.translated_text: Having attained conjunction with the rays of the Sun through their penetrating quality, they illumine

children.text: pārśvāṇi sarvāṇi anurañjayanti guṇaiḥ upetāḥ sphaṭik[ādayaḥ hi] ||
children.translated_text: all sides far and wide with their clusters of rays — crystals and such, endowed with [excellent] qualities.

body.text: yat
body.translated_text: That which is heard in legends that gems themselves dispel darkness — that legend is merely a laudatory statement.

body.text: upākhyānādiṣu ratnāni eva dhvāntam dhvaṃsayanti iti śrūyate tat upākhyāna[m arthavādamātra]m eva |
anye punar anyathā manyante ã
body.translated_text: Others, however, think otherwise:

body.text: svacchāyayā arkasāmīpyāt vikalendusamīkṣaṇam |
body.translated_text: The observation of an incomplete Moon is due to its own shadow, because of proximity to the Sun.

body.text: iti | svacchāyayā candraḥ śuklaḥ upalabhyate, tasya śuklasya candramasaḥ savitṛsannikarṣāt vaivarṇyam bhavati iti | kutaḥ etat? yadi svabhāvataḥ śuklasya candramasaḥ sūryasannikarṣāt vaivarṇyam syāt tadā śuklapratipadādiṣu candrasya aparabhāgaḥ vivarṇaḥ syāt sūryasannikarṣāt, na pūrvabhāgaḥ | tathā ca avāṅmukham candrabimbam upalakṣyate | tasmāt mithyājñānam eva etat yat saugataiḥ ucyate || 5 ||
body.translated_text: That is: the Moon appears bright by its own nature, and due to the proximity of that bright Moon to the Sun, discoloration occurs. How is this [possible]? If the naturally bright Moon were to become discolored due to proximity to the Sun, then on the first day of the bright fortnight and thereafter, the far side of the Moon should be discolored due to proximity to the Sun, not the near side. And thus the Moon's disc would be observed facing downward. Therefore, this is nothing but false knowledge — that which is asserted by the <s>Saugatas</s> (Buddhists). || 5 ||

body.text: bhūgolasaṃsthānam
body.translated_text: The shape of the Earth-globe

body.text: bhādikakṣyābhūsaṃsthānapradarśanāya āha ã
body.translated_text: In order to demonstrate the arrangement of the stellar sphere, the orbits, and the shape of the Earth, he says:

children.translated_text: In the middle of the circular stellar cage, encircled by the orbits, situated at the center of space,
composed of earth, water, fire, and air, the Earth-globe is round on all sides. || 5 ||

body.text:
bhāni jyotīṃṣi nakṣatrāṇi | teṣām bhānām pañjaraḥ bhapañjaraḥ | yasmāt [bhāni] samantataḥ viyati pañjarasthāni iva lakṣyante tataḥ anena darśanena etat uktam | vṛttaḥ ca asau bhapañjaraḥ ca vṛttabhapañjaraḥ | vṛttabhapañjaramadhyam, madhyam antaḥ, tasya vṛttabhapañjarasya | tatra vṛttabhapañjaramadhye | kakṣyāpariveṣṭitaḥ kakṣyābhiḥ grahāṇām pariveṣṭitaḥ kakṣyāpariveṣṭitaḥ | khamadhyagataḥ, kham ākāśam, tasya madhyam khamadhyam, khamadhyaṃgataḥ
khamadhyagataḥ, ākāśamadhyasthaḥ iti yāvat | katham ākāśamadhye nirālambanā bhūḥ avatiṣṭhate? [ucyate ã svabhāva]prādhānyāt; yathā salilāgnivāyavaḥ kledadahanapreraṇātmakāḥ, na teṣām anyaḥ asti kaścit kledadahanapreraṇaprayojakaḥ, evam iyam api bhūḥ dhāraṇātmikā, na ca dhāryamāṇātmikā | athavā patantī bhūḥ, "patatu adhaḥ" iti āha | atha kim idam adhaḥ nāma | yathā asmadīyānām pṛthivī adhaḥ, evam pṛthivyāḥ kim adhaḥ? "adhaḥ"-śabdaḥ ca digvācī,
diśaḥ ca vyavasthāpekṣayā bhavanti | yathā yatra vivasvān udeti sā prācī, yatra astam eti sā parā, yasyām adṛśyaḥ gacchati sā uttarā, śeṣā dakṣiṇā | āsām antarāleṣu eva vidiśaḥ | evam upari adhaḥ ca pṛthivī apekṣayā bhavataḥ | tena tasyāḥ pṛthivyāḥ na kiñcit upari, na adhaḥ, tasmāt patanābhāvaḥ bhuvaḥ | evam ca pṛthivyāḥ ardham pariveṣṭyā avasthitaḥ samudraḥ na patiti | patantyām ca bhuvi loṣṭaśilīmukhādayaḥ viyati kṣiptā na bhuvam āsādayeyuḥ | bhūḥ mandam
patati iti cet, sādhyate ca etat māyāvidbhiḥ ca, viyati khātakīlakaḥ anāśrayaḥ bhavet | atha anye manyante ã śeṣeṇa anyena [vā] bhūḥ dhriyate iti | tat uktam | śeṣādīnām api avaśyam ādhāraviśeṣaḥ kaścit kalpanīyaḥ, [taya anyaḥ ā]dhāraḥ syā[t tasya api anyaḥ] iti anavasthā | atha te svaśaktyā eva avatiṣṭhante iti cet, bhuvaḥ eva kasmāt sā śaktiḥ na parikalpyate | tasmāt jagataḥ dharmādharmāpekṣayā sarvabhūtadhātrī bhūḥ niścalā ākāśe tiṣṭhati | mṛjjalaśikhivāyumayaḥ
bhūgolaḥ, pratyakṣam yataḥ upalabhyate | sarvataḥ vṛttaḥ | mṛdādinā kāṣṭhādinā vā ayaḥśalākāyām madhye samavṛttavat avagantavyaḥ | asya bahiḥ candrādīnām kakṣyāḥ darśayitavyāḥ || 6 ||
body.translated_text: <s>Bhāni</s> means luminous bodies, that is, <s>nakṣatras</s> (asterisms). Their cage is the <s>bhapañjara</s> (stellar cage). Because the stars are observed all around in the sky as if situated in a cage, this expression is used for that reason. It is circular and it is a stellar cage, hence <s>vṛttabhapañjara</s> (circular stellar cage). The middle of the circular stellar cage means 'inside' — that is, inside of that circular stellar cage. There, in the middle of the circular stellar cage. Encircled by the orbits — encircled by the orbits of the planets, hence <s>kakṣyāpariveṣṭita</s> (orbit-encircled). Situated at the center of space — <s>kha</s> means the sky, its middle is the center of space, situated at the center of space means stationed in the middle of the sky. How does the Earth remain unsupported in the middle of space? It is said: by the predominance of its inherent nature. Just as water, fire, and wind have the nature of moistening, burning, and impelling, and there is no other agent causing their moistening, burning, and impelling, so too this Earth has the nature of supporting, and is not one that is supported [by something else]. Alternatively, the Earth is falling — let it fall downward, one might say. But then what is this thing called 'downward'? Just as for us the earth is below, what is below the earth? The word 'below' denotes direction, and directions exist only with reference to a relative framework. As where the Sun rises is the east, where it sets is the west, where it goes unseen is the north, and the remainder is the south. The intermediate directions are in the intervals between these. Similarly, 'above' and 'below' exist only with reference to the Earth. Therefore, for that Earth there is nothing above or below it, and hence there is no falling of the Earth. And thus the ocean, which stands surrounding half of the Earth, does not fall. And if the Earth were falling, clods, arrows, and the like thrown into the sky would not reach the ground. If one objects that the Earth falls slowly — well, this would also be accomplished by illusionists, and a peg planted in the sky would remain unsupported. Now, others think: the Earth is held up by <s>Śeṣa</s> or by some other [being]. To that it is said: for <s>Śeṣa</s> and others too, some particular support must necessarily be postulated, and for that another support, and for that yet another — leading to an infinite regress. If they stand by their own power, then why should that same power not be attributed to the Earth? Therefore, the Earth, which supports all beings in accordance with <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) of the world, stands motionless in space. Composed of earth, water, fire, and air — the Earth-globe, as is directly perceived. Round on all sides. It should be understood as uniformly round, like [a ball] made of clay or wood mounted on an iron rod at its center. Outside of this, the orbits of the Moon and others are to be shown. || 6 ||

body.text: bhūgolapṛṣṭhe prāṇinām sthitiḥ
body.translated_text: The position of living beings on the surface of the Earth-globe

body.text: bhūgolapradarśanāya āha ã
body.translated_text: In order to illustrate the Earth-globe, he says:

children.translated_text: Just as the flower-head of a <s>kadamba</s> blossom is densely covered on all sides with florets,

children.text: tadvat hi sarvasattvaiḥ jalajaiḥ sthalajaiḥ ca bhūgolaḥ || 7 ||
children.translated_text: so indeed is the Earth-globe [covered] with all living beings, both aquatic and terrestrial. || 7 ||

body.text: yadvat kadambapuṣpagranthiḥ [samantāt kesaraiḥ] pracitaḥ, vyāptaḥ iti arthaḥ, tathā ayam bhūgolaḥ samantāt jalajaiḥ sthalajaiḥ ca prāṇibhiḥ āvṛttaḥ | atha ye bhuvi vyavasthitāḥ prāṇinaḥ parvatādayaḥ teṣām katham avasthānam tat ucyate ã yatra yatra prāṇinaḥ gacchanti tatra tatra teṣām bhūḥ eva adhaḥ, viyat upari pratibhāti yathā asmākam || 7 ||
body.translated_text: Just as the flower-head of a <s>kadamba</s> blossom is densely covered — that is, pervaded — on all sides by filaments, so this Earth-globe is surrounded on all sides by aquatic and terrestrial living beings. Now, as for those living beings and mountains and such that are situated on the Earth, how is their positioning? It is stated thus: wherever living beings go, there the Earth alone appears below them, and the sky above, just as it does for us. || 7 ||

body.text: bhuvaḥ vṛddhyapacayau
body.translated_text: The growth and diminution of the Earth

body.text: bhūvṛddhyapacayajñānāya āha ã
body.translated_text: In order to explain the growth and diminution of the Earth, he says:

children.translated_text: In one day of <s>Brahmā</s>, there is a growth of one <s>yojana</s> above the surface of the Earth.
In one night equal to that day, there is a diminution of the earth that has been accumulated. || 8 ||

body.text: tṛṇakāṣṭhabhasmādirūpeṇa vidyamānāyāḥ [bhuvaḥ] yojanavṛddhiḥ bhavati | ataḥ eva gṛhapādapataḍāgādikhāteṣu ghaṭapiṭakādi upari upari avayavāḥ labhyante |
body.translated_text: There is a growth of one <s>yojana</s> of the Earth in the form of grass, wood, ashes, and so forth. For this very reason, in excavations of houses, trees, ponds, and the like, fragments of pots, baskets, and such are found at higher and higher [layers].

body.text: dinatulyayā ekarātryā brahmadivasatulyayā rātryā | mṛdupacitāyāḥ bhavati hāniḥ | mṛdā upacitā mṛdupacitā, tasyāḥ mṛdupacitāyāḥ hāniḥ bhavati | kena punar kāraṇena yat upacitam buvaḥ tat parikṣīyate? brahmadivasāvasāne kila saṃvartakābhidhānaiḥ jaladharaiḥ vicchinnadhārābhimuktena payasā yat upacitam bhuvaḥ tat parikṣīyate || 8 ||
body.translated_text: In one night equal to the day — in one night equal to a day of <s>Brahmā</s>. There is a diminution of the earth that has been accumulated. <s>Mṛdupacitā</s> means accumulated with earth; of that accumulated [earth] there is diminution. By what cause, then, is what has been accumulated on the Earth consumed? At the end of a day of <s>Brahmā</s>, by clouds called <s>saṃvartaka</s> (dissolution clouds), through water released in unbroken streams, what has been accumulated on the Earth is consumed. || 8 ||

body.text: bhūpramāṇam
body.translated_text: The measure of the Earth

body.text: bhūbhramaṇavācakapūrvottarapakṣapratipādanāya āha ã
body.translated_text: In order to present the prior and subsequent positions regarding the statement about the rotation of the Earth, he says:

children.text: anulomagatiḥ nausthaḥ paśyati acalam vilomagam yadvat |
children.translated_text: Just as one moving in the same direction on a boat sees a stationary [object on the bank] as moving in the opposite direction,
so the stationary stars, moving uniformly westward, [are seen] at <s>Laṅkā</s>. || 9 ||

body.text:
anulomagatiḥ nausthaḥ, kaścit anulomagatiḥ nausthaḥ, paśyati acalam, na calam vastugatyā api sthiram, vilomagam yathā paśyati saritsāgarobhayataṭasthitam vṛkṣadikam, [tathā eva] ca bhūmau prāṅmukham bhramatyām upari[sthitāḥ janāḥ] nabhasthitāni acalāni bhāni pratilomagāni aparagāni paśyanti | tathā hi laṅkāsthāḥ bhāni samapaścimagāni paśyanti | laṅkā upalakṣaṇamātram | evam anye api paśyanti | tasmāt iyam bhūḥ eva prāṅmukham bhramati
| niścalam jyotiścakram | bhūgatyā taduparisthitaḥ yaḥ bhacakrapradeśaḥ purastāt sa udayan iva ca lakṣyate, yaḥ tu madhye sa gaganamadhyasthitaḥ iva, yaḥ hi dūreṇa saḥ astam gacchan iva lakṣyate | anyathā hi niścalasya bhacakrasya udayāstāsambhavaḥ syāt |
body.translated_text: One moving in the same direction on a boat — some person moving in the same direction while on a boat sees a stationary object — not moving by the motion of the object, but actually fixed — as moving in the opposite direction, just as he sees trees and such situated on both banks of a river or ocean. In the same way, when the Earth rotates eastward, those situated upon it see the stationary stars in the sky as moving in the opposite direction, that is, westward. Thus, those stationed at <s>Laṅkā</s> see the stars moving uniformly westward. <s>Laṅkā</s> is merely illustrative; others too see them likewise. Therefore, this Earth itself rotates eastward; the stellar sphere is motionless. Due to the motion of the Earth, that region of the stellar sphere which is ahead appears as if rising, that which is in the middle appears as if stationed at the zenith, and that which is far away appears as if setting. Otherwise, for a motionless stellar sphere, rising and setting would be impossible.

body.text:
idam asya ādarśanam | bhūmaṇḍale bhramati [sati] jagat jaladhinā āplāvet, bhūgolavegajanitaprabhañjanena ākṣiptāḥ taruśikharaprāsādādayaḥ viśīryeran | pakṣiṇaḥ api viyati utpatan na svanīḍam āsādayeyuḥ | tasmāt dharitrībhramaṇe na kiñcit liṅgam asti | tasmāt anyathā vyākhyeyam sūtram | yathā anulomagatiḥ nausthaḥ puruṣaḥ calavastūni vilomagam paśyati, evam bhāni calāni pravahānilākṣiptāni vegavaśāt laṅkāyām yāni vastūni tāni pratilomagāni
paśyanti; adhovyavasthitām bhuvam niścalām bhramantīm iva paśyanti | pratyakṣe api nakṣatrāṇi prāguditāni aparām diśam āsādayanti || 9 ||
body.translated_text: This is the refutation of that [view]. If the Earth's disc were rotating, the world would be flooded by the ocean; trees, mountain peaks, palaces, and the like, hurled by the storm generated by the Earth-globe's velocity, would be shattered.
